Kim Morrison said:

(Tongue in cheek, but if we went with those tactic names we should also make simply X a macro for simpa using X... :-)

Posting this in a separate thread, but I personally think that the current semantics of simpa using h is bad/code smelly. IIUC, the semantics of simpa using h is

  • simplify h and the target
  • (semireducibly) run exact h

Example:

def foo := 37
example (n : ℕ) (h : foo = n) : 37 = n := by simpa using h

This means that:

  • adding simp lemmas might break simpa calls: maybe you only simplify h or the target in a non-defeq way, and now simpa fails. There is a built-in violation of the flexible tactic linter within this tactic
  • the exact might be unexpectedly expensive.

I would personally love it much more if the semantics of simpa using h became simp at h; simp [h]. This has some increased flexibility (the goal doesn't have to reduce exactly to h, but can use h), and should be stable under adding (confluent) simp-rules.
( @Kim Morrison )

I've additionally noticed that simpa using h sometimes fails where have := h; simpa succeeds. I think this is because of some elaboration order stuff. My instinct is that we should force h to be fully elaborated before starting to simplify it, but that does break some existing uses of simpa which use the goal type to elaborate the hypothesis.

I would love to see the experiment of replacing simpa with this behaviour in Mathlib (or rather, a hook that runs both new and old behaviour and compares), and count the failures.

I don't think such a change would be unreasonable to make, if that evidence looks okay, and we have a reasonable plan for backward compatibility. (Perhaps initially simpa could use the new behaviour, with a fallback to the old behaviour and a warning? And then turn off the fallback a version later? And a set_option backward for another version or two?)

The proposed change is doing two things at once

  1. Reduce what simpa can do by restricting to reducible transparency.
  2. Expand what simpa can do by passing the hypothesis as a simp argument.

I think we should first do (1) before we can think about (2)

There's another thread about simpa going on here: #lean4 > silly simpa bugs @ 💬

Something that comes to mind regarding simpa using h is that the way it could work instead, which would be more consistent, is that if the goal is |- g, then simpa using h would prove the goal |- g = h, and if that succeeds, it closes the original goal. This avoids all the defeq issues. It's also more restrictive.

Possibly we might want to deprecate simpa using itself and create a new simp_exact tactic. It's a bit odd how simpa using is "simp and close with assumption, but use this for the assumption, and it can be a complex term".

For Floris's proposal, I almost want to suggest simp [args...] using [args...] as a possible extension to simp itself. The idea would be that the using clause args would be simplified using the first simp set, and then added to the simp set.
my usage of simpa is only as a exact_mod_simp tactic, so I always have a using which is fed any arbitrary term which simp should be able to prove its type matches the goal type

Kyle Miller schrieb:

Possibly we might want to deprecate simpa using itself and create a new simp_exact tactic. It's a bit odd how simpa using is "simp and close with assumption, but use this for the assumption, and it can be a complex term".

I would be interested in why you would want to use such a simp_exact tactic over your suggested simp [args..] using [args2..]

@Moritz Roos Sometimes simp_exact e can be more meaningful. If I read simp [e], I'd think "ok, e is used in some way to simplify the goal". If I read simp_exact e, I'd think "ok, e is basically a proof of the goal, up to some simplification".

There are also cases where simp_exact e succeeds and the proposed simp using [e] would fail. It's possible for e to be a proof of an equality, and as such it would be used for rewriting. What if it's e : 2 = f 2? Then simp using [e] would diverge, rewriting all 2's in the goal with f (f (... (f 2) ...) ), forever.

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

  1. Reduce what simpa can do by restricting to reducible transparency.

I've now tried this in #13636.

The Mathlib adaptation branch is at lean-pr-testing-13636 (on the mathlib4-nightly-testing fork), and is currently failing. (Also failing in Batteries actually, same branch name.)

Options:

  1. Someone, not me, goes through those branches fixing the problems.
  2. I wrap each of the failure sites with set_option backward.simpa.using.reducibleClose false in, and these are added to the technical debt reports.
  3. We drop this.

My preference and default if I don't hear otherwise is 2.

Another option, since simpa is a terminal tactic (and hence it's okay to do more expensive things), is to have simpa try the unification at reducible transparency, and if that fails try again automatically at default transparency, but print a warning.
Do you know how many cases would need fixing? Can you generate (2) automatically?

I just vibe coded a python script to do (2) automatically.

  1. It gets the lake build log
  2. greps for Type mismatch: After simplification errors
  3. wraps each failure with set_option backward.simpa.using.reducibleClose false in
    I'm running it on a loop on lean-pr-testing-13636.
    https://github.com/Deicyde/simpa-wrapper

Right now I'm counting 775 in Mathlib across 452 files. Build is at 8380/8380 but failing. I will report back when it compiles.

update: Just hit 1000 sites and still not compiling. This would be a very large refactor.
There's an existing tool to do this, by the way, that might be more robust: scripts/add_set_option.py.

Thank you! Yes, this is definitely much more optimized than my implementation. For what it's worth, my hand-rolled script just finished running. Final result:

  • 1942 set_option backward.simpa.using.reducibleClose in Mathlib across ~1100 files
  • 15 in Batteries
  • 7 build errors on lean-pr-testing-13636 which can not be resolved by set_option backward.simpa.using.reducibleClose and need to be manually fixed.

I'm going to run it again with scripts/add_set_option.py and see if the result is any different.

Just finished running scripts/add_set_option.py. Turns out the 7 build errors mentioned above were due to my original buggy implementation of the script. Final build compiles with 2212 backward.simpa.using.reducibleClose across 1309 Mathlib files. I will run rm_set_option.py to double check that all of them are strictly necessary. PR can be found here: https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4-nightly-testing/pull/216
And also the Batteries PR: https://github.com/leanprover-community/batteries/pull/1797
Thanks for running that experiment!

I presume our conclusion here is that this is too many set_option backward, and we don't actually want to proceed with this change to simpa.

(Although I guess a further useful experiment would be "Claude, how many of these set_option backward can you remove the need for without doing anything ugly.")
Is it too many?
Not for me: so if you'd be happy with that number too, perhaps we can keep pushing here!
I think the important question is how easy these are to fix. If most of these are just missing a simp lemma, the we should fix them. But if they are harder to fix, then it might be more problematic.
@Kim Morrison Instead of set_option backward.simpa.using.reducibleClose, could you make this available via simpa!? Then I would certainly love to have this in Mathlib.

Unfortunately we can't do this, I think, as simpa! already means something! The exclamation mark on simp tactics turns on the autoUnfold config option, which uses all equational lemmas, even for semireducible definitions. It isn't used much in Mathlib (34 times), but nevertheless we can't steal this syntax without a bigger change, I think.

(We could just repurpose simpa! to have this new meaning, and not have it call simp! internally, but this feels very confusing.)

What about

  • simpa using! h
  • simpa using h at default

?
esimpa (analogous to erw)?
I'd prefer simpa using! h over esimpa

I was discussing the syntax with @Anne Baanen yesterday. I see roughly two options:

  1. We try to repurpose tac! to always mean tac, but with more aggressive unfolding
  2. We have a longer-form and readable (to newbies!?) modifier. Atm there is with_reducible and friends, but I think those are quite unintuitive to everyone who hasn't studied defeq transparencies.

I don't have a good suggestion for (2), beyond the exactly and definitionally that Kim offered in #mathlib4 > distinguishing different types of `exact`

About option 1 (! meaning more unfolding), we have the following tactics in Mathlib with ! variant. While controlling reducibility seems to be the plurality interpretation, the only consistent meaning seems to be "work harder".

  • #count_heartbeats! (runs #count_heartbeats multiple times and averages the result)
  • abel!, abel1!, abel_nf! (controls the reducibility)
  • by_cases!, by_contra!, contrapose!, wlog! (original tactic followed by push Not)
  • cases_type!, casesm! (prohibition on creating more subgoals)
  • choose! (omit parameters from the new functions if possible)
  • clear! (clear also hypotheses that depend on the ones given to clear!)
  • compute_degree!, monicity! (does norm_num <;> try assumption on the goals left by compute_degree)
  • congr! (more powerful congruence algorithm compared to congr)
  • dsimp!, simp!, simpa! (arguably controls the reducibility but unfolds much more aggressively than other !s)
  • itauto! (add classical logic)
  • linarith!, nlinarith! (controls the reducibility)
  • reduce_mod_char! (searches harder for CharP instances)
  • rw!, rewrite! (insert casts to make dependent rewrite work better)
  • ring!, ring1!, ring_nf! (controls the reducibility)
  • set! (does less: don't replace the original expression with the variable)
  • use! (apply constructors everywhere, not just right-associative)

And #39039 would introduce convert!, convert_to! and ac_convert! (controls the reducibility)
(Note: I counted these by looking for !s on the tactic documentation page. If the ! option is not documented then I wouldn't be able to see it.)

I am also wondering if by_cases!/by_contra!/contrapose!/wlog! should be the default, since I don't think push Not ever does the wrong thing, per se. It might just not do anything useful. Especially for contrapose! and by_contra! we use them more or less half of all times anyway (according to these inaccurate numbers obtained by grep $tac | wc -l for various values of $tac):

  • by_cases!/by_cases: 397/5072 ~ 7,8%
  • by_contra!/by_contra!: 519/1187 ~ 43,7%
  • contrapose!/contrapose: 839/1324 ~ 63,4%
  • wlog!/wlog: 52/420 ~ 12,3%

Caveat: I made no effort to only search inside tactic calls. Probably for contrapose and wlog we'd have them show up in natural language too, so their actual ratio might be higher (i.e. we'd be using ! more than these estimates).
So, should we make push Not the default and free up ! for another meaning here? Or maybe someone has another symbol idea? ring$ because it's more expensive?
Yes please! I have been wanting this for a long while
Another improvement that comes to mind is to allow referring to assumptions in contrapose using the french quotes \f<>. This is useful to contrapose on a typeclaas assumption without naming it

There is a reason to not run push Not after by_cases. If your goal involves if a < b then _ else _, it is a common approach to split into cases with by_cases h : a < b <;> simp [h]. This proof breaks if we push negation into a < b.

  1. We have a longer-form and readable (to newbies!?) modifier. Atm there is with_reducible and friends, but I think those are quite unintuitive to everyone who hasn't studied defeq transparencies.

Is with_allow_unfolding less unintuitive?
Certainly better
If our goal is to move away from the "unfold more" variants, then I think something that is visually easier to catch in review than a terminal ! would be helpful.
perhaps a short go! tactic is a nice intermediate?
i'm only half joking, btw. i think it'd be neat if we added this shortcut for with_reducible or some variant.

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

There is a reason to not run push Not after by_cases. If your goal involves if a < b then _ else _, it is a common approach to split into cases with by_cases h : a < b <;> simp [h]. This proof breaks if we push negation into a < b.

But surely one should just have a tactic that does the cases AND substitutes in the if then else? split_ifs is almost that, except it doesn't allow specifying which condition to split over, in case the location contains several if then elses

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

There is a reason to not run push Not after by_cases. If your goal involves if a < b then _ else _, it is a common approach to split into cases with by_cases h : a < b <;> simp [h]. This proof breaks if we push negation into a < b.

Isn't this what split is for?
When you have multiple ifs, then split sometimes doesn't target the one you want to split.
Doesn't split not let you name the hypothesis?

Oh I'm just referring to something like (if a < b then 3 else 45) + (if c < d then 31 else 2) where split won't let you split c < d. Anyways, I suppose the argument for by_cases h : a < b <;> simp [h] generalizes to goals with a < b in it in any way, not just if, in which case split doesn't help.

Ok lean#13636 now changes the behaviour of simpa, and provides the simpa using! h syntax for the old behaviour. The lean-pr-testing-13636 branches at both Batteries and Mathlib are happy, so I think we can proceed here.

I'm happy to see all the work above. If we're going to keep using ! as a tactic modifier, I hope it has consistent, or at least easy-to-learn/understand-in-each-special-case semantics. I'm worried we're making it do many things...
(I needed to teach the flexible tactic linter about this new syntax, because for bootstrapping reasons the old syntax declaration still exists.)
using! is a nice solution for the naming question, I like the change!

#39039 seems to pick up merge conflicts before the build even passes. What do we think about the following approach to getting it into Mathlib without tearing my hair out over conflicts?

  • We make a preparatory PR introducing only the convert! syntax, which can be used by #39039 and #38071.
  • We make a PR (a series of them, grouped per-folder maybe?) replacing convert with convert! everywhere. This would be easy to check automatically since the diff will only read - ... convert ... + ... convert! .... Maybe here we also PR the "Try this" suggestions generated by #39039, where convert! does the same as convert. Or maybe in a separate PR?
  • Finally, we PR the logic change inside convert! from #39039 and #38071 as two final PRs, when the risk of them going stale is a lot lower.
Ah --- so the point is that at step (2), convert! does literally the same? That's a neat way to do it; I like it!

Anne Baanen said:

  • Finally, we PR the logic change inside convert!

Did you mean that we change the logic in convert and keep convert! the same?
